newsitem.title: INDIA: Germany will press ahead with reforms - Rexrodt.
newsitem.headline: Germany will press ahead with reforms - Rexrodt.

text.p: The German government will continue to pursue free-market economic reforms despite some domestic resistance, and push for more open global trade, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Thursday.

Rexrodt told the Sixth Asia-Pacific Conference of German Industry and Trade that Germany recognised that capital and expertise were more mobile than ever, and had introduced reforms to attract investment.

"We need to deregulate and cut costs to hold our own in the competition for investment," he said. The German government had already implemented some measures and others were under discussion, he said without elaborating.
"Of course, there is resistance from those who will lose privileges," he said.
"But we shall stick to our policy of reform. There is no alternative."
Rexrodt, who inaugurated the two-day conference with Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, said Germany would not allow itself to be deflected from its policy of open markets.
He said Germany would push for further liberalisation of world trade in a ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation set for December in Singapore.
"Beyond that, we shall also be calling in Singapore for progress on the new trade policy issues, such as investment protection and competition," Rexrodt said.

Rexrodt said German companies seeking to compete for business in Asia had certain advantages over rivals, including expertise in environmental and transport technology, which he called two sectors "with a genuine future".
But he said Germany's university system must be made more attractive for foreign students to promote more contact between nations which is needed to make cross-border business partnerships work.

"We must find solutions for the many problems facing foreign students in Germany," he said, citing long courses of study, the fact foreign degrees are not always recognised in Germany, legal impediments on foreigners in Germany and the language barrier.
"If we succeed, let us hope that more young people will again come from Asia to study in Germany," he said.
